data.title: House Ethics Committee adopts rule changes around sexual misconduct investigations
data.description:
The House Ethics Committee voted Thursday to adopt a collection of rule changings seeking to expedite sexual misconduct investigations within the lower chamber and increase transparency throughout the process.

The panel unanimously passed the changes, which include granting its leadership subpoena authority, streamlining deadlines for respondents to address an investigative subcommittee’s findings and codifying its “policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct.”

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that the process for the members themselves who are under the purview of this committee, that that due process is protected,” Rep. Michael Guest (R-Miss.), who chairs the committee, said in the public session before the vote.

Lawmakers from both parties have called for faster Ethics Committee investigations into sexual misconduct as a string of high-profile cases involving House members intensified scrutiny of the panel’s often-secretive process.

One of the more recent prominent cases involved outgoing Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), whose ex-girlfriend accused him of harassment and threatening to release explicit images of her. Another woman Mills dated initially told police he assaulted her in February 2025 before recanting.

Mills, who is leaving his post in January after losing in his state’s GOP primaries, has denied all allegations of wrongdoing. The Ethics panel has been investigating him since November 2025.

The Ethics Committee also said earlier this year it was investigating reports that Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) violated House rules by “engaging in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer.” Gomez told The Hill in an August statement his actions “were consensual in nature and haven’t violated the law or House Ethics rules.”   

Former Reps. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) and Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), who had both been accused of sexual misconduct, were under investigation when pressure to resign from both sides of the aisle contributed to their departure from Congress in April. 

And more recently, House lawmakers voted to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) in September after a damning Ethics report found he demonstrated “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” Edwards dropped his midterm reelection bid after the panel released its findings.

House Ethics Committee Ranking Member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) said he hopes the rule changes will reinforce the committee’s “commitment to the integrity of the House of Representatives on sexual harassment.”

“We’re hoping that all of these changes will reflect positively on the committee, and they should, and our staff, but also in the House as we do these improvements and look at further ways to make sure that the process is fair, transparent, and people are held accountable,” he added.

data.title: Fiona the Hippo dies days after ingesting hat, Cincinnati Zoo announces
data.description:
CINCINNATI (WDTN) – Fiona the Hippo has died after eating a hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident, the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Gardens.

The zoo announced Fiona’s death Thursday afternoon on social media.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” reads a message the zoo posted to Facebook.

“The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week.  Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”

The zoo had explained several days ago that a visitor had accidentally tossed the hat into Fiona’s habitat. (NewsNation reported that the hat hit a ceiling fan before going into the hippo’s enclosure.) The staff was “cautiously optimistic” that Fiona would pass the hat on her own and monitored her around the clock.

In their latest post, they asked Fiona’s fans to “keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her” in their thoughts.

“We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are.”

After the initial incident, zoo staffers warned visitors to keep their personal items secure, and to alert a worker if any potentially harmful objects ended up in the enclosures.

Fiona, 9, was born Jan. 24, 2017 to Bibi and Henry. Her half-brother, Fritz, was born in 2022.

data.title: 70 percent of Americans back targeted tariffs on steel: Poll
data.description:
A majority of Americans support targeted tariffs on foreign steel, according to new data.

Seven in 10 of the respondents to the Harris Poll survey, obtained exclusively by The Hill, said targeted tariffs should be part of the federal government’s approach to maintaining strong domestic steel production capability.

About 8 in 10 Republicans and 6 in 10 Democrats backed targeted tariffs on steel imports, per the survey.

President Trump imposed tariffs on steel imports during his first term, under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 — which allows the president to tax imported goods on national security grounds.

Former President Biden maintained those levies, and Trump increased them from 10 percent to 50 percent in the early months of his second term.

The president has also threatened to slap 50 percent tariffs on Canadian imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting on Jan. 1, 2027, amid his trade war with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Scott Paul, the president of the Alliance for American Manufacturing, said the need for the federal government to protect the domestic steel industry “transcends partisan politics.”

“Congress must recognize that targeted steel trade measures not only have broad bipartisan public support but are essential as American workers and manufacturers continue to fight rampant unfair trade and global overcapacity,” Paul added in a release announcing the results of the Harris Poll survey.

Roxanne Brown, the president of United Steelworkers International, also said “strategically placed tariffs” must be part of the federal government’s approach to allow domestic industries “to compete on a level playing field.”

The Harris Poll conducted its survey from Nov. 5-7, polling 1,802 registered voters. The overall results had a margin of error of 2.8 percentage points.

Democrats this midterm cycle campaigned on reining in Trump’s tariff authorities, as the levies contributed to elevated costs for Americans.

Roughly 6 in 10 respondents to a recent Reuters survey said they want Congress — which Democrats will control come January — to repeal the president’s import levies.

data.title: Cryptocurrency industry stares down new Congress: 5 takeaways from Capitol Crypto Forum
data.description:
The cryptocurrency industry is facing a political reckoning as Democrats with a more skeptical view of digital assets prepare to take control of Congress, casting uncertainty about the industry’s legislative prospects.

As the industry scrambles to make inroads with the incoming majority following the midterms, the uncertain future of crypto policy loomed over The Hill and The Block’s “Capitol Crypto Forum” on Thursday, where lawmakers and industry leaders were divided over the prospects for reviving stalled legislation.

The crypto world had a powerful ally in President Trump and a GOP-controlled Congress after a series of clashes with Biden-era regulators. Trump-appointed regulators eased federal oversight of digital assets, numerous investigations were dropped against digital asset firms and Republicans-passed landmark legislation establishing the first regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But after the Clarity Act, a major crypto regulation bill, failed to pass the Senate, insiders agree that the chances to revive the effort are slim. Now, the industry is bracing for what’s next from the newly Democratic-controlled committees and crypto’s future in Washington.

Here are five takeaways from Thursday’s event, which was sponsored by Bitget, Block, Inc. and Latham & Watkins.

Cautious optimism for the next Congress

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), chair of the House Financial Services Committee, pointed to the 78 Democrats who backed the Clarity Act in the House as evidence that the industry still has allies across the aisle.

“We had a lot of support from Democrats, both on the House and Agriculture Committee and the House Financial Services Committee, and I expect that’ll continue in the new Congress,” Hill said.

Hill said he was encouraged by a memorandum from Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), who is hoping to succeed him as chair, outlining digital asset market structure as an issue she intends to work on.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), a co-sponsor of the Clarity Act, pointed to an unlikely partnership with longtime crypto critic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) as someone on the Democratic side to help advance crypto legislation.

“I’ll blow all your minds. I’ve had conversations with Elizabeth Warren, where she says, ‘I want the industry regulated. I just don’t want the industry to write the regulations,’” Moreno said, praising Warren for being “very, very smart” and “very thorough.”

Rep. Steve Horsford (D-Nev.), who is the lead sponsor of the PARITY Act, was also optimistic that a bipartisan agreement could be reached, but stressed that lawmakers must address concerns about ethics and transparency.

“We do need to get the legislation right,” Horsford said. “I just hope that everyone stays at the table.”

The future of the Clarity Act

The Clarity Act’s failure to pass the Senate in September left many of its backers questioning whether Congress squandered its best opportunity to pass its most important item in crypto’s legislative agenda.

Hill said he regretted the decision to separate the Clarity Act from the GENIUS Act, the stablecoin legislation signed into law last year, arguing that prolonged negotiations allowed new demands to pile up and made reaching an agreement increasingly difficult.

“I had urged the Senate and the administration last summer to have Clarity [Act] and GENIUS [Act] passed together in the House, and I still stand by that. I think it would have been the right decision,” he said. “I regret that they were separated.”

Stu Alderoty, the chief legal officer at technology company Ripple, acknowledged that the disagreements within the cryptocurrency industry also complicated negotiations, citing disputes over stablecoin rewards and the Trump family’s involvement in crypto “overwhelming the conversation.”

“I think the industry can do a better job of speaking with one voice,” he said.

Regardless, most agreed that with just weeks left for the 119th Congress, the odds were not favorable of a revamped version of the bill passing anytime soon.

Crypto caught in the political crossfire

The crypto industry poured millions into this year’s midterm elections, aggressively throwing their support behind crypto-friendly candidates in more than 100 races across the country.

Despite its heavy spending in the midterms, the industry still faced crushing defeats in key races, including spending $55 million against Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) who defeated incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

At Thursday’s forum, Moreno lamented how cryptocurrency regulation had become entangled in partisan politics.

“The industry should have never gotten sucked into the political vortex,” Moreno said. “This isn’t a Democrat or Republican issue in my mind.”

Peter Van Valkenburgh, the executive director of Coin Center, pointed to another political divide: the Democratic Party’s internal debate over its approach to the emerging technology.

“There’s a battle for the soul of the Democratic Party with respect to tech policy,” Van Valkenburgh said, pointing to the increasing skepticism around artificial intelligence and other forms of advanced technology.

He argued that Democrats who are in favor of technological innovation have struggled to counter the party’s more skeptical and louder voices.

“There’s a very strong anti-tech vision being articulated in parts of the Democratic Party, and the voices for a tech-forward Democratic Party, they haven’t found their song yet,” he said.

Could regulators step in where Congress couldn’t?

With the Clarity Act stalled, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) could take the lead in establishing clearer regulatory rules.

Moreno argued that regulators could accomplish much of what Congress failed to do through formal rulemaking.

But Hill was less convinced, warning that agency regulations could face lawsuits and be reversed by future administrations.

“It’s not a permanent fix,” Hill said. “It’s subject to litigation. It does not have the force of law.”

Kristin Smith, a cryptocurrency industry advocate and interim CEO of Blockchain Association, noted that regulators may be better positioned to tackle the complexities of digital asset policy.

“The learning curve for your average member of Congress or staffer is huge,” she said, pointing to the SEC and CFTC’s expertise in regulating financial markets.

She suggested that allowing agencies to develop rules now could make it easier for Congress to address remaining gaps through more focused legislation in the future.

Prediction markets tout election accuracy

Prediction markets emerged from the midterms with a strong showing, correctly predicting a significant portion of races.

Brian Quintenz, a board member at prediction market platform Kalshi, praised the betting markets’ accuracy in predicting the outcome of the midterm elections, arguing that they provided voters with valuable information as results came in.

“I think the markets did an incredible job,” he said, adding that the results showed prediction markets’ ability to assess polling data and accurately price election results.

The former CFTC commissioner pointed to the Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska, where prediction markets quickly signaled the shock Democratic upsets from Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D) and Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D), respectively, as votes began to be counted.

“You had markets providing a very clear signal about what was going to happen, what did happen, in a way that I think actually added credibility and integrity to those outcomes,” he said. “In my mind, a huge success.”

But the industry’s rapid growth has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers concerned about market manipulation and insider trading from those who could profit from their access to crucial information.

data.title: Judge says Rollins' religious holiday messages likely violated First Amendment
data.description:
A district court judge on Thursday said U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins likely violated the First Amendment after sending emails to her staff about Jesus Christ, God, Christmas and Easter.

Rollins had sent out four holiday-related emails, which prompted federal employees to file a lawsuit in May. U.S. District Court Judge Trina Thompson agreed with the employees on the emails referring to Christmas and Easter.

The Biden-appointed judge wrote in her ruling that Rollins’s “good faith intentions … are not the issue here.”

“The April 5, 2026, and Dec. 23, 2025, messages go too far,” Thompson wrote. “They suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an Establishment Clause violation.”

She elaborated that protecting “private devotion and spiritual reflection from government influence comes to the fore.”

“The wisdom of the Founders was in recognizing that independence requires freedom of conscience,” she continued. “The command of the Establishment Clause, thus, is to prohibit the government from using its authority to try to sway an individual’s decision about whether and how to practice their faith … this court requires the Secretary to observe her own directives.”

The Easter email told USDA employees that God had “granted each of us victory and new life. And where there is life –– risen life –– there is hope.” The email begins with “Happy Easter — He is Risen indeed!”

Thompson said the comparison between employees and “the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago” portrays “the agency’s work as a mission to serve her particular Christian views.”

The Hill has reached out to the USDA for comment.

Politico first reported on the Easter message earlier this year, when USDA employees claimed the messages made them “feel excluded and unwelcome, and they fear the negative consequences of not sharing the Secretary’s religion or expressing their own different beliefs in the workplace.”

Rollins has been very open about her Christian faith, posting excerpts of scripture on social media. She also takes part in Bible study groups with other Trump Cabinet members,

The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment prohibits the federal government from establishing any official religion or showing preference to any one religion over others. It was also established to prohibit state-sponsored churches like the Church of England, according to the U.S. Courts website.

The amendment’s Free Exercise Clause protects people’s right to practice their own religion as long as it does not run afoul of a “compelling” governmental interest, citing the 1944 Prince v. Massachusetts decision. The Supreme Court ruled at the time that the state could force children to be inoculated despite parents citing their faith as against inoculation.

data.title: Hunter Biden slams Trump for 'great betrayal' after calling Putin 'friend'
data.description:
Hunter Biden, the son of former President Biden, went after President Trump over referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend.”

“The Great Betrayal. Of the allies who trusted us. Of the soldiers who served. Of every American who believed the office was larger than the man,” Biden said in a post on the social platform X Thursday afternoon.

“[Trump] stands for nothing but himself. History will hold both of these men accountable for their crimes,” he added.

Biden’s post featured a screenshot of a headline from the BBC about Trump’s comments.

The president greeted Putin as a “friend” on Thursday, as the two arrived for a meeting in China.

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying, after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Trump has a notably friendly relationship with Putin in spite of tension between Washington and Moscow in the last decade. The president was set to speak separately with Putin during a visit to Shenzhen, China, aside from a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Putin and Trump’s meeting marks their first-one-on-one since an August 2025 summit in Alaska, which was meant to further negotiations on the Russia-Ukraine war.

Trump told reporters earlier this week that he thought the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit a five-year mark in February.

“I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” the president said. “I think he’s backing down. I think he’d like to, frankly, I think he’d like to see it finished.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

data.title: Meta brings fight over Washington state campaign ad law to Supreme Court
data.description:
Meta is asking the Supreme Court to hear its challenge to a Washington state law requiring that social media companies answer public requests for information about the political advertisements shown on their platforms.

The company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said in a petition docketed Wednesday the law is “virtually unprecedented” and violates the First Amendment by unreasonably restricting political speech. 

“Had Washington simply banned political ads from digital platforms altogether, that would be an obvious First Amendment violation,” Meta’s lawyers wrote in court filings. “The result should be no different when a state achieves the same end via the most burdensome political-ad disclosure regime in the Nation.” 

Washington amended its Fair Campaign Practices Act in 2018 to require that Meta and other “digital communication platforms” collect demographic, impression and audience data for qualifying political ads in the state. Upon a request, they must provide the information within two business days. Penalties for not doing so can reach up to $30,000 per violation. 

The state attorney general’s office, which declined to comment on Meta’s latest filing, has defended the law in court by saying it’s necessary to inform voters.

Meta responded by banning political ads in the state, though the company has since conceded that some records requests had slipped through and that it didn’t adequately respond to these inquiries from members of the public.

Washington sued the tech giant, and a state judge ordered Meta to pay nearly $25 million plus legal fees. It’s appealing the decision after its arguments fell flat before Washington’s top court. 

The Supreme Court chooses which cases it hears and turns away the vast majority of petitions. The justices are likely to consider Meta’s request at a closed-door meeting later in the term.

The company is represented by Paul Clement, a veteran Supreme Court advocate who served as former President George W. Bush’s top representative before the court. 

Clement said the First Amendment concerns with Washington’s law couldn’t be “overstated” and told the justices their intervention is needed to resolve a split with a court that considered similar law in Maryland and ruled the other way.

“Shutting down political speech in ways that are not politically neutral is as antithetical to First Amendment values as it gets,” Clement wrote in court filings. “And our Constitution does not permit states to impose prohibitive compelled-speech mandates on media companies and then fine them tens of millions of dollars when they inevitably cannot perfectly comply.”

The Washington attorney’s general office declined to comment on Meta’s appeal and pointed to its existing court papers.

data.title: Baltimore Mayor blasts Marlon Humphrey after Raven's 'criminals' comment
data.description:
The mayor of Baltimore blasted Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey for comments the defensive back made on a podcast earlier this week disparaging the city.

Humphrey was asked during a recent episode of his podcast what Baltimore “is the best at making.”

“Criminals,” he responded before bursting out into laughter.

The comment was met with widespread condemnation online and earned him a rebuke from his team, which sent Humphrey home from the team’s trip to North Carolina to take on the Panthers this weekend.

The defensive back apologized for the comment after practice according to ESPN on Wednesday saying “as you guys know, I’ve been here my whole career. Spent lots of offseasons here. Welcomed a son here and I’m an investor in the city. And obviously, I do know the effect that words have and just like to apologize for those comments.”

Baltimore’s mayor Brandon Scott (D) was not satisfied.

“While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough,” Scott said. “Baltimore is a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives and to have someone that looks like them who wears a Baltimore Ravens jersey relegate them to becoming criminals cuts deeper.”

He added, “I wonder how he would feel if prominent Baltimoreans used their platforms to imply that Baltimore once produced great defensive backs, but we have recently lost our way.”

The mayor also noted he was inviting Humphrey “to sit down with me and some Baltimoreans who have re-entered into our community and are now preventing others from making the mistakes they made.”

Humphrey was one of several Ravens who attended a recent trip President Trump made to the Baltimore area before the midterm elections.

The Ravens won four of their first five games this season but lost to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers on Monday.

data.title: Sanders pours cold water on 2028 White House bid
data.description:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has poured cold water on the idea of another run for the White House. 

“I think probably not. I think taking office at 87 years of age and finishing my first term at 91 is not something that probably inspires a whole lot of people,” Sanders told host Steven Bartlett on “The Diary of a CEO” podcast. 

He later doubled down: “No, I’m not running for president.” 

The Vermont senator described his ideal candidate as someone “prepared to stand with the Working class of America” and “take on the oligarchs,” adding that he would not support a candidate “tinkering around the edges.” 

Sanders has been in Congress since 1991, spending more than a decade in the House before winning his Senate seat in 2006. He ran for president in the 2016 presidential election but lost the Democratic nod to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton — then tried again in the 2020 cycle, dropping out to pave the way for former President Biden. 

The progressive won a fourth term in 2024 and has cited his age in contending that he won’t likely seek a fifth term in 2030. 

Asked in a 2024 interview with Politico whether this would be his last term in Congress, Sanders said: “I’m 83 now. I’ll be 89 when I get out of here. You can do the figuring. I don’t know, but I would assume, probably, yes.” 

Sanders also told Barlett this week that it’s “not a good idea” to treat elections like “beauty contests.” 

“The American people have to determine: what is their view on healthcare? Are they going to transform our healthare system? What are they going to do on AI? These questions … And then leadership will come to the fore based on how people res- feel that these candidates are responding,” he said. 

He heaped praise on Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), a progressive leader on Capitol Hill who has been increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender.

“But she’s not the only one. There are great other candidates that are out there who may not be quite as wellknown,” Sanders said. 

“You don’t know who’s going to rise up. The point that I’m making is …  I’m not a fan of what you’re doing here,” he told Barlett. “I am a fan of: here are the issues. How are the candidates going to address them? People will decide.”

data.title: Appeals court denies full panel review of McIver bid to toss case
data.description:
The Third Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday declined a request from Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) to have a full panel of the court weigh her bid to dismiss her pending charges after a scuffle outside an immigration detention facility.

McIver has pushed to get the case dismissed on various grounds, including that her visit to the Delaney Hall detention facility was carried out in her role as a legislative official and should be protected by prosecution under the Speech or Debate Clause. 

But in August, a three-judge panel for the court declined to toss the case, even as the panel split over a matter in which she is accused of attacking law enforcement with her forearms.

A brief notice from the court gave no rationale for the decision beyond noting the bench voted not to take up the case.

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power—but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in a statement.

“Now, due to the disappointing decision by the Third Circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

McIver could appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court, and the lawmaker said in her statement that she and her legal team “are looking at every possible option for what comes next.”

Over the summer the three-judge panel declined to toss the case on a number of grounds raised by McIver, finding that while her inspection of Delaney Hall was protected under the clause, her intervention in the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) was not.

But one judge dissented, saying McIver’s “plausibly incidental contact” with one of the officers came as she was being impeded from carrying out her legislative duties by touring the controversial detention center.

He also touched on McIver’s claims that the case amounted to a selective prosecution, saying the lawmaker “presented enough [evidence] to obtain discovery on whether this prosecution ‘was intended to prevent [her] exercise of a fundamental right’” to conduct legislative oversight.

McIver is now slated to face trial in the case, though an earlier trial date set for this month has not been rescheduled while motions were pending.
